newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian PM fights for survival after ally quits.
newsitem.headline: Indian PM fights for survival after ally quits.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda was set on Monday to fight a grim battle to ride out a political challenge from a former ally.
Congress president Sitaram Kesri set the crisis in motion for Deve Gowda's 10-month-old government on Sunday when he withdrew his party's backing for the centre-left coalition.

"I met the President (Shankar Dayal Sharma) today and told him that we are withdrawing support to the United Front government and I also staked our claim to form a (new) government," Kesri told a news conference later on Sunday.
Congress politicians said Kesri was expected on Monday to ask President Sharma, the constitutional head of state, for a chance to form a new government.

The ruling United Front's decision-making Steering Committee was also scheduled to meet on Monday to discuss the next move, which could include a plea to Sharma to allow Deve Gowda to face parliament when it meets after a month's recess on April 21.
Kesri's bombshell decision overshadowed delicate peace talks between India and Pakistan and threatened to stall Deve Gowda's budget for fiscal 1997/98, still to be approved by parliament.
Indian stock prices dropped sharply in off-market kerb deals on Sunday on fears that Deve Gowda might have to resign and call a snap mid-term election.
The ruling coalition said it would stand firm.
"There is no question of the resignation of Mr Deve Gowda," United Front spokesman Jaipal Reddy told reporters.
"We are solid, we are one. There is no question of a new government."
Stockbrokers in the commercial capital Bombay said it was unclear how Congress, which has only 140 deputies in the 545-seat Lok Sabha or lower house of parliament, could form a government.
"If Congress is taking a gamble on this one, it will be interesting to see how they will come out," said Rupa Bose, strategist at Paribas Capital Markets in Singapore.
Some brokers predicted a steep plunge on the Bombay Stock Exchange on Monday.
Kesri became Congress president in September after former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao was forced to resign the post over corruption charges.
But he did not appear to have the backing of several key Congress leaders, including influential former defence minister Sharad Pawar.
Pawar, regarded as a supporter of Deve Gowda's government, said he had been kept in the dark about Kesri's move.
The ruling alliance looked more united with nearly all its key constituents, including Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's Tamil Maanila Congress, saying they fully backed Deve Gowda.
Chidambaram's group broke away from the Congress last year and analysts said Kesri was clearly hoping it would return to the fold.
India's oldest political machine, Congress is reeling from a string of financial scandals dogging its leading politicians.
Congress officials said the withdrawal decision followed "attempts by the United Front" to split the Congress party in the key north Indian state of Uttar Pradesh.

The rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) formed a coalition government in the state earlier this month, thwarting Congress attempts to rule the crucial region which sends 85 deputies to the lower house of parliament.
Deve Gowda's alliance, which groups free-traders, communists and centrists and controls some 178 deputies in the lower house, was formed in June 1996 after inconclusive national elections.
A leading opinion poll last month predicted major gains for the BJP against both the United Front and the Congress if mid-term polls were held soon.
